hints: Think about what level of organisation a gene is - it is not a whole chromosome or a protein, but a small section of a molecule found in the nucleus.
Focus on what that DNA section does - what product is made from its code during protein synthesis.
walkthrough:
What molecule genes are made from**
Think of chromosome 11 as a very long DNA molecule. A gene is just one short length along that molecule, made of a specific sequence of nucleotide bases - A, T, C and G.

What the sequence is for**
That base sequence carries the code to make one polypeptide chain. For example, the catalase gene codes for the polypeptide that folds to form the enzyme catalase. So gene = DNA sequence coding for polypeptide.
Final answer: A gene is a sequence of DNA nucleotides that codes for a polypeptide.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.1 and compare the two new strands - one is made continuously toward the fork, the other is made in short pieces away from it. What does this tell you about how new nucleotides are added?
Recall how a new nucleotide is chosen - what rule pairs it with the exposed template strand?
Think about the backbone of DNA - what strong bond links one nucleotide to the next in the same strand?
Consider why one strand is discontinuous - what small fragments need to be stitched together, and on which strand?
Remember you must cover both enzymes to gain full credit - check you have a distinct joining role for DNA ligase separate from building the strand.
walkthrough:
DNA polymerase builds the new strand**
DNA polymerase adds activated (phosphorylated) free nucleotides one by one. It selects them by complementary base pairing to the exposed template - A with T, C with G - as seen in Fig. 4.1.

Joining nucleotides together**
The enzyme forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, so the polynucleotide chain elongates in the direction shown by the arrows. It also proofreads the new strand and can remove mismatched bases.

DNA ligase finishes the lagging strand**
Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand (the lagging strand) is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase joins these fragments together by forming phosphodiester bonds to complete the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone.

Final answer: DNA polymerase adds activated nucleotides complementary to the template strand, forming phosphodiester bonds to elongate the new polynucleotide strand and proofreads the new strand. DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, forming phosphodiester bonds to complete the sugar-phosphate backbone.

hints: Recall interphase has three stages - two gap phases for growth and one middle phase where the S stands for making an exact copy of DNA.
walkthrough:
Placing replication in the cell cycle**
Interphase is G1 then S then G2. DNA must be replicated before mitosis so each daughter cell gets a full copy. That synthesis of new DNA happens in the S phase, where S means synthesis.
Final answer: S phase (synthesis phase) of interphase.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.2 - find the central dot where the two chromatids meet and the lines pulling sideways to the cell. Which one holds things together and which one does the pulling?
Think about metaphase to anaphase - what needs to line up at the equator first, then be pulled apart to opposite poles?
walkthrough:
Structure A - the central join**
A is the centromere in the middle of the metaphase chromosome. It holds the two sister chromatids together and is where spindle fibres attach via the kinetochore.

Structure B - the pulling threads**
B is the spindle fibres made of microtubules. In metaphase they attach to the centromere and hold chromosomes at the spindle equator. At the start of anaphase they shorten and pull the separated chromatids to opposite poles.

Final answer: Structure A - centromere: holds sister chromatids together and is site of attachment to spindle fibres. Structure B - spindle fibres (microtubules): orientate chromosomes at the equator in metaphase and separate chromatids / move them to opposite poles in anaphase.

hints: Start from Fig. 4.2 at metaphase with two chromatids joined - what must happen to that join for anaphase to give identical sets to each end?
Picture the centrioles at each end of Fig. 4.3 - how should each separated chromatid be connected to them, and what shape does a chromatid make when pulled by its centromere?
Remember detail matters for the drawing - each moving chromatid is now a single chromosome, so show its own centromere clearly.
walkthrough:
Split into two identical units**
In anaphase the centromere divides and sister chromatids of chromosome 11 separate. Draw two separate single-stranded chromatids, one on the left side moving to the left centrioles and one on the right side moving to the right centrioles. This ensures each daughter nucleus gets one identical copy.

Show the spindle pulling**
Draw thin spindle fibre lines from each chromatid to its nearest pole/centrioles as shown by the centriole symbols in Fig. 4.3.

Correct chromatid shape**
Draw each single chromatid V-shaped or U-shaped with the centromere at the point leading toward the pole, because it is being pulled by its centromere. Mark a dot for the centromere on each chromatid.

Final answer: Draw two separate single chromatids, one moving to each pole. Each chromatid attached by spindle fibres to the pole/centrioles, drawn V-shaped or U-shaped with point/centromere leading toward the pole. Centromeres marked on both chromatids.
